learn: Voice is the recognisable way an artist sees and makes: subjects, materials, marks and ideas.
Voice grows through practice, experiment and reflection.
Influences are normal; voice is how you transform them.
lessons.try: Collect ten of your past works and describe what they share.

learn: Every artist has a lineage of influences.
Study three artists whose work speaks to you.
Note what you take from each and what you reject.
check: You can ___ parts of an influence.
lessons.try: Make an influence map with images and notes.

learn: Try unfamiliar materials, scales and methods.
Failures teach as much as successes.
Keep experiments in your sketchbook.
lessons.try: Make five quick experiments in unfamiliar media.

learn: A sustained investigation explores one inquiry across 15 or more works.
Questions should be open: "How can everyday objects show memory?"
Choose something you can explore for months.
check: Choose a question you can explore for...
lessons.try: Write three possible inquiry questions and choose one.

learn: Show growth through practice, experimentation and revision.
Document process with photos and notes.
Let each work inform the next.
lessons.try: Plan the first five works in your investigation.

learn: Write brief statements about inquiry, materials and revisions.
Explain choices, not just describe them.
Be concise and specific.
lessons.try: Write 100 words explaining one revision.

learn: Marks can be gestural, controlled, rhythmic or broken.
Line weight conveys emotion and depth.
Artists like Käthe Kollwitz used powerful, expressive marks.
lessons.try: Fill a page with twenty kinds of marks.

learn: Charcoal, graphite, ink, pastel, conté and digital tools.
Each medium has its own range of value and texture.
Combine media for richness.
lessons.try: Draw one subject in four different media.

learn: Drawing records ideas, plans and observations.
Diagrams, maps and notes are forms of drawing.
Contemporary artists exhibit drawings as finished works.
lessons.try: Make a visual map of an idea.

learn: Simultaneous contrast: colours change appearance next to each other.
Josef Albers studied colour interaction.
Colour relationships create harmony or tension.
lessons.try: Make a colour study showing simultaneous contrast.

learn: Acrylic dries fast; oil dries slowly and blends; watercolour is transparent; gouache is opaque.
Use solvents safely or choose water-based options.
Experiment with surfaces: canvas, panel, paper.
lessons.try: Compare a small study in acrylic and watercolour.

learn: Combine paint with collage, drawing, text or found materials.
Layer intentionally to build meaning.
Archival materials make work last.
lessons.try: Make a mixed-media piece for your investigation.

learn: 3D work uses mass, volume, space and surface.
Negative space is part of sculpture.
Barbara Hepworth pierced her forms to include space.
lessons.try: Make a maquette (small model) for a sculpture.

learn: Clay, wood, cardboard, wire, plaster, textiles and found objects.
Joining methods: slotting, gluing, tying, welding (with training).
Safety first with tools.
lessons.try: Build a sculpture from cardboard using slots.

learn: Installations shape how viewers move and feel.
Light, sound and time can be materials.
Document installations with photos and video.
lessons.try: Design an installation and document a model.

learn: Photographers make deliberate choices about subject, framing and light.
Series and sequences tell stories.
Alfred Stieglitz argued photography was fine art.
lessons.try: Shoot a ten-image sequence for your investigation.

learn: Digital painting, 3D modelling, animation and video.
Free tools include Krita, Blender, GIMP and Inkscape.
Digital work needs file management and backups.
lessons.try: Create a digital work and save layered versions.

learn: Get consent before photographing people for exhibition.
Respect copyright; use public domain or licensed material.
Be transparent about editing and AI-generated content.
lessons.try: Write a personal code of ethics for image-making.

learn: Present work with a short statement of intent.
Listeners describe, analyse, interpret and suggest.
Take notes and thank critics.
check: Present work with a statement of...
lessons.try: Lead a critique of your own work.

learn: Meet with a teacher or mentor to discuss direction.
Prepare questions in advance.
Set next steps.
lessons.try: Prepare three questions for a mentor conference.

learn: Remove weak pieces; strengthen the core.
Fill gaps with new works.
Sequence work to show development.
check: Revising a body of work removes...
lessons.try: Edit your body of work down to the strongest pieces.

units.t: Writing About Art: The Artist Statement

learn: A statement helps viewers understand your work.
It explains what, how and why.
It should sound like you.
check: A statement explains what, how and...
lessons.try: Read five artist statements and note what works.

learn: Start with your inquiry or main idea.
Describe key materials and processes.
End with what you hope viewers experience.
check: End with what you hope viewers...
A typical statement is about ___ words.
lessons.try: Draft a 250-word artist statement.

learn: Cut jargon and vague words.
Read aloud for flow.
Use statements for exhibitions, portfolios and applications.
lessons.try: Revise your statement with peer feedback.

learn: Choose your strongest, most varied and most personal work.
Include both sustained investigation and range.
Follow the requirements of each programme.
lessons.try: Select 15-20 works for a portfolio.

learn: Use even daylight or two lights at 45°.
Shoot straight on, crop cleanly, colour-correct.
Include detail shots for texture.
lessons.try: Photograph five works professionally.

learn: Create a clean website or PDF portfolio.
Title, medium, size and year for every work.
Keep files organised and backed up.
check: Every work should list title, medium, size and...
lessons.try: Build a digital portfolio and share it.

units.t: Exhibition and Life After High School

learn: Choose a title, theme and space.
Plan layout, labels, lighting and publicity.
Coordinate installation and take-down.
lessons.try: Plan a senior exhibition with classmates.

learn: Talk with visitors about your work.
Gather feedback and contacts.
Document the show.
lessons.try: Practise a 30-second talk about your work.

learn: Paths: art school, university, community college, apprenticeships, self-taught practice.
Careers: illustration, design, animation, teaching, curating, art therapy, architecture.
Keep making art whatever path you choose.
lessons.try: Research three arts careers and their training.
